newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope rests at halfway mark as Poles mull message.
newsitem.headline: Pope rests at halfway mark as Poles mull message.

text.p: Pope John Paul rested in his beloved Tatra mountains on Thursday, midway through a sentimental journey he is using to prod Poles into exercising their new economic and political freedoms justly.
On the sixth day of his trip, the 77-year-old Polish Pope had no public engagements in the area where he loved to relax and meditate as a young man, priest and bishop.
He was billeted in a secluded Church-owned retreat in the highland resort of Zakopane, his privacy jealously guarded by Polish and Vatican security officials.

Local officials in the area of snow-capped peaks, bubbling streams and wooden chalets prepared a series of easy itineraries for the Pope, who was an avid hiker and skiier until 1994, when he slipped in his bath and broke his leg.
Two helicopters left the area near the house, indicating that the Pope had probably been taken to an even more isolated mountain area for part of his private day.
The Tatra region of sweeping vistas is precious to the sometimes frail Pope, who appears reinvigorated by the scent and feel of his homeland and the rapturous welcome of more than a million Poles.
"This trip certainly has recharged his batteries," said Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls. "It's very clear that he is very happy to be home."
The Pope's "day off" will give both him and his countrymen a pause to take stock of the messages he has been hammering since arriving on Saturday for his seventh trip home.
Speaking like a concerned but stern father, he has expressed deep worry about some changes since Poland became the first Eastern European country to cast off communism in 1989.

While the Pope has congratulated Poles on their economic achievements since then, he has warned of a moral wilderness and a get-rich-quick mentality as the once-centralised economy soars to new heights.
Realising that Poles themselves are questioning their country's direction, the Pope has pulled no punches on some of the most burning issues dividing them, chiefly abortion.
He railed against the practice on Wednesday in the central city of Kalisz, saying economically and culturally successful societies were still barbarian if they allowed it.

Whether abortion should remain liberalised or be restricted again has become a key issue in the campaign for September's elections, in which a powerful alliance centred around the pro-Catholic Solidarity union is rivalling the ruling ex-communists.
"A nation which kills its own children is a nation without a future," he told Poles in one of his most emotional remarks.
Another theme has been the fate of Poles impoverished during the country's dizzying economic development.
As in other post-communist countries, economic change has left many in its wake and created a new class of people more adept at capitalism's rough-and-tumble rules.
The Pope warned that a new wall of economic and political selfishness had arisen in Europe and was threatening the unity of the continent just as much as the Berlin Wall did before communism's fall.
When he arrived in Poland last Saturday, President Aleksander Kwasniewski, an ex-communist, asked the Pope to help build bridges and not walls between political opponents.
The Pope has responded with a series of forceful challenges to the government on social issues that may influence the political debate after he returns to the Vatican on June 10.
